oxymoron

ok-see-MOR-on -- from Greek oxys ('sharp') + moros ('foolish, dull') -- literally 'sharply foolish.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Oxymoron is a figure of speech that combines two normally contradictory terms.

During the debate, one student pointed out that the phrase 'controlled chaos' in the opposing team's own slogan was itself an oxymoron.

Example

When the waiter described the tiny appetizer as a 'jumbo shrimp,' the whole table laughed at the obvious oxymoron.

'Jumbo' and 'shrimp' contradict each other directly -- pairing two opposite ideas in a single phrase is exactly what makes something an oxymoron.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

incongruity: An incongruity is any mismatch — a tuxedo at a beach picnic, a cheerful tune at a solemn ceremony. Nothing about it needs to be deliberate or even spoken. An oxymoron is a crafted figure of speech: two contradictory words fused on purpose into one phrase.

antithesis: Antithesis places two opposing ideas side by side in balanced phrasing — 'it was the best of times, it was the worst of times.' The opposites stay separate and contrasted. An oxymoron fuses its opposites into a single compressed phrase, so the clash lives inside one expression.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

consistency: logical agreement between parts, with no contradiction

harmony: agreement in feeling, opinion, or effect

Where it sits · how deep the clash of ideas goes

contradiction → oxymoron → paradox

contradiction vs. oxymoron: A contradiction is milder than an oxymoron: it is simply two claims that clash, while an oxymoron sharpens the clash by fusing contradictory terms into one deliberate, jarring phrase.

paradox vs. oxymoron: A paradox goes further than an oxymoron: an oxymoron compresses its clash into a two-word phrase, while a paradox — like the gentle general's fearsome reputation — poses a deeper contradiction that whole arguments try to untangle.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix/root — oxy-: sharp, acid (Greek (oxys))

root — -moron: foolish, dull (Greek (moros))

Put it together: Oxymoron literally means 'sharply foolish' in Greek -- oxy- ('sharp') plus moros ('foolish, dull'), a fittingly self-contradictory name for a phrase built from two contradictory words.

Use the root in a new word: moron: The English word moron was actually coined directly from the Greek moros in the early 1900s as a clinical term, before it became a common insult.

Word Building

Word Choice

Oxymoron is a precise literary term for pairing two contradictory words on purpose, like 'deafening silence' or 'act naturally' -- it's not just a general word for any weird or confusing statement.
